plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels labeled (a), (b), and (c) that illustrate the process of gaseous diffusion as two initially separated gases mix after a connecting stopcock is opened. In panel (a), 'Stopcock closed,' all small white dots representing H2 molecules are confined to the left bulb and all red dots representing O2 molecules are densely packed in the right bulb, with the closed stopcock valve preventing any exchange. In panel (b), 'Stopcock open,' a small number of white H2 molecules have already dispersed into the O2-side bulb while fewer red O2 molecules have crossed to the H2 side, reflecting the faster diffusion rate of the lighter, less massive H2 gas. In panel (c), 'Some time after Stopcock open,' both white and red dots are distributed approximately uniformly across both bulbs, indicating that the concentration gradients have largely equalized through continued random molecular motion. This figure demonstrates that diffusion is driven by concentration gradients and that lighter gases diffuse more rapidly than heavier ones, motivating the quantitative relationship described by Graham's law of effusion.

demo_steps.title: Separated gases
demo_steps.narration: With the stopcock closed, white H2 particles are confined to the left bulb and red O2 particles are confined to the right bulb. No diffusion occurs because the gases cannot pass through the closed valve.

demo_steps.title: Stopcock opened
demo_steps.narration: Once the stopcock opens, particles begin crossing the connecting tube. More H2 has moved into the O2 bulb than O2 has moved into the H2 bulb because H2 is lighter and diffuses faster.

demo_steps.title: Continuing random motion
demo_steps.narration: As time passes, both gases continue spreading through both bulbs. The net movement follows the concentration gradients even though each molecule moves randomly.

demo_steps.title: Uniform mixture
demo_steps.narration: Some time after opening the stopcock, both H2 and O2 are distributed approximately uniformly across both bulbs. Diffusion has reduced the concentration differences that drove the initial net movement.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Diffusion is random molecular motion with a directional net effect: gases spread from high to low concentration, and lighter gases spread faster.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a horizontal two-bulb glass apparatus similar to the source figure: pale cyan transparent circular bulbs connected by a narrow tube and a central stopcock. At time 0, show all white H2 particles in the left bulb and all red O2 particles in the right bulb with the stopcock visibly closed. As elapsed time increases, open the stopcock and move particles through the tube into the opposite bulb; H2 should redistribute faster than O2, so early frames show many white particles in the right bulb but fewer red particles in the left bulb. At maximum time, distribute both particle colors nearly uniformly across both bulbs. In molecular-mass-emphasis mode, visually highlight H2 as lighter/faster, such as brighter or cooler coloring plus longer faint motion trails, while O2 appears heavier/slower, such as darker red with shorter trails. Preserve the original panel logic through phase captions or status labels: closed, open/early diffusion, and some time after opening.

authoredContext:
In general, we know that when a sample of gas is introduced to one part of a closed container, its molecules very quickly disperse throughout the container; this process by which molecules disperse in space in response to differences in concentration is called diffusion (shown in ). The gaseous atoms or molecules are, of course, unaware of any concentration gradient, they simply move randomly—regions of higher concentration have more particles than regions of lower concentrations, and so a net movement of species from high to low concentration areas takes place. In a closed environment, diffusion will ultimately result in equal concentrations of gas throughout, as depicted in . The gaseous atoms and molecules continue to move, but since their concentrations are the same in both bulbs, the rates of transfer between the bulbs are equal (no net transfer of molecules occurs).

Explain why the numbers of molecules are not identical in the left- and right-hand bulbs shown in the center illustration of .

(a) Two gases, H 2 and O 2 , are initially separated. (b) When the stopcock is opened, they mix together. The lighter gas, H 2 , passes through the opening faster than O 2 , so just after the stopcock is opened, more H 2 molecules move to the O 2 side than O 2 molecules move to the H 2 side. (c) After a short time, both the slower-moving O 2 molecules and the faster-moving H 2 molecules have distributed themselves evenly on both sides of the vessel.

In this figure, three pairs of gas filled spheres or vessels are shown connected with a stopcock between them. In a, the figure is labeled, “Stopcock closed.” Above, the left sphere is labeled, “H subscript 2.” It contains approximately 30 small, white, evenly distributed circles. The sphere to its right is labeled, “O subscript 2.” It contains approximately 30 small red evenly distributed circles. In b, the figure is labeled, “Stopcock open.” The stopcock valve handle is now parallel to the tube connecting the two spheres. On the left, approximately 9 small, white circles and 4 small, red circles are present, with the red spheres appearing slightly closer to the stopcock. On the right side, approximately 25 small, red spheres and 21 small, white spheres are present, with the concentration of white spheres slightly greater near the stopcock. In c, the figure is labeled “Some time after Stopcock open.” In this situation, the red and white spheres appear evenly mixed and uniformly distributed throughout both spheres.

discrepancies: The middle panel is labeled 'Stopcock open' but in the default state it still shows separated gases and appears effectively closed; the source middle panel shows the stopcock open with partial mixing already underway.

The particle distribution in panel (b) is conceptually wrong at default: the source has red and white particles in both bulbs, while the generated figure keeps H₂ mostly/all in the left bulb and O₂ mostly/all in the right bulb.
Extra status text, legend, and faint motion arrows are added inside the figure area even though the source is a clean static three-stage diagram without these annotations.
The generated figure is visually compressed by the side control panel, making the textbook diagram much smaller than the source and reducing the legibility of particles and labels.
The stopcock/valve artwork is simplified and inconsistent across panels, especially because the generated middle panel does not visually match the open stopcock state shown in the source.
evaluation.notes: The overall three-panel diffusion apparatus is recognizable and the controls are meaningful, but the default middle panel contradicts the source and the added annotations/UI compression hurt its use as a drop-in static replacement.

Force the panel (b) valve to render as open whenever it is labeled 'Stopcock open', rather than tying it to a slider value of zero.
Remove or hide the added status text, legend, and motion arrows in the default view, or move them to optional interactive mode only.
Rebalance the layout so the three apparatus panels occupy most of the available width and labels/particles are comfortably readable at inline size.
